source.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
source.authors: N. Koriagin; Yaroslav Aksenov; Daniil Laptev; Gleb Gerasimov; Nikita Balagansky; Daniil Gavrilov

record.tranche_reason: Tests the LLM/SAE-feature part of the claim with domain-specific SAE reconstruction and feature-interpretability analyses, not the original toy-network superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE reconstruction metrics and SAE-derived feature examples and interpretability scores. It does not test overlap geometry, feature orthogonality, neuron polysemanticity, or whether SAE features are canonical units. Layer choice and top-k settings used in the experiments are not outcomes.
record.test_reason: A methods paper. It uses SAEs as a tool and reports how well its own residual 'SAE Boost' adapts them to new domains: explained variance (EV), LLM cross-entropy (CE) and interpretability scores against a pretrained SAE or other adaptation methods. It does not test whether LLM features are superposed, toy-model geometry, the causes of polysemanticity, whether SAE features are canonical, or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: residual SAEs trained on a pretrained SAE's domain reconstruction errors improve domain EV and CE, and change general-domain metrics by less than 1%. The authors also claim the method beats other domain-adaptation methods on the general/domain/sparsity trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a residual SAE on reconstruction errors from pretrained LLM SAEs; it does not use the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that residual SAE training duration affects general-domain EV: fewer than 100M tokens can reduce it by up to 31%, while after 200M tokens the reported change is less than 1%. Increasing residual top-k raises domain EV while also increasing L0 sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: General-corpus SAEs reconstruct domain text poorly. Pretrained EV is 0.348–0.693 on domain/language data vs 0.719 on FineWeb-Edu (Tables 1, 2, 5). A residual SAE trained on those errors adds features with low cosine similarity to the base features (Fig. 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionaries trained on general corpora are incomplete for domain-specific features ('feature blindness'). This bears loosely on the 'complete' part of V5, but the paper reports it as motivation and baseline performance, not as a test.

record.problems: The study does not measure superposition geometry, neuron-level feature distribution, or SAE feature stability and completeness. Most reconstruction results report no uncertainty. The base and residual feature sets in Table 10 were evaluated on different datasets, limiting interpretation of their score comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 general-domain performance results and Tables 3-4 and 6-9 method-comparison and multi-domain results were not separately cataloged; they focus on preservation or adaptation-method comparisons rather than the feature-recovery evidence represented by the selected domain reconstruction rows. Figure-based similarity and t-SNE analyses were not included because they do not directly measure whether SAE features recover the named domain concepts.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of it: no capacity analysis of neurons.
All of it: no alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Not tested as a claim. SAEs are assumed to recover features; no neuron-level spreading analysis and no test of whether sparse features exist.
Stability and canonicity not tested. Completeness is touched on only incidentally, via the 'feature blindness' motivation.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' and its V4 'supports' label are rejected. Every row compares the paper's own method to a baseline, which the rules exclude as evidence on a version. The paper treats SAE feature recovery as given and evaluates a domain-adaptation technique, so it is T4 (uses without test).

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure explains polysemantic neurons or causes important features to receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests SAE recovery and interpretation of features in selected LLM activation data, but not feature spreading across neurons or whether this is representative across LLMs generally.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

relation.reason: It uses sparse dictionary representations as an interpretability tool and reports its adaptation method's performance.

tranche.reason: The study develops SAE domain adaptation and evaluates reconstruction, sparsity, and interpretability performance; it does not independently test a superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: R13 repeats R5's Russian EV values; Table 5 does not explicitly identify its backbone. The authors' less-than-1% general-domain claim holds for EV and CE in Table 2, but not all L0 values: Qwen Chemistry increases from 50 to 51 and Llama UN Debates from 55 to 56.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested SAE configurations on Chemistry Data, Russian Texts, and UN Debates; cross-lingual EV results; and the listed chemistry feature examples
reader_labels.reason: SAE reconstructions improve EV and LLM CE across the reported domain/model combinations, and the paper provides examples of SAE Boost features interpreted as domain-specific concepts (R1-R19, R22-R26).
